questions.question: What is Backtracking?
options: An algorithm that always moves forward without revisiting choices
A brute-force technique that randomly shuffles the search order
A systematic search algorithm that builds a solution incrementally and abandons a partial solution as soon as it determines it cannot lead to a valid complete solution
A technique for sorting elements using a recursive pivot
questions.explanation: Backtracking explores a solution space incrementally and prunes branches early ('backtracks') when a partial solution violates constraints — avoiding unnecessary full exploration.

questions.question: What does pruning mean in algorithms?
options: Removing duplicate elements from an array
Eliminating branches of the search tree that cannot possibly lead to a valid solution, reducing unnecessary computation
Sorting the input before processing it
Reducing the recursion depth by converting to iteration
questions.explanation: Pruning cuts off parts of the search space early when constraints are already violated, dramatically reducing the number of states the algorithm needs to explore.

questions.question: How does backtracking differ from brute force?
options: Backtracking is always faster because it sorts data first
They are identical — backtracking is just a formal name for brute force
Backtracking uses pruning to abandon invalid partial solutions early, while pure brute force generates and evaluates all complete candidates
Brute force uses recursion; backtracking does not
questions.explanation: Pure brute force generates every complete candidate before checking validity. Backtracking checks validity incrementally and abandons branches as soon as a constraint is violated — often far more efficient.

questions.question: What is a permutation?
options: A selection of elements where order does not matter
An arrangement of all elements of a set in a specific order, where every arrangement is considered distinct
A subset of elements chosen without replacement
A sorted version of the original sequence
questions.explanation: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of elements. For n distinct items, there are n! possible permutations — order matters.

questions.question: What is a combination?
options: An ordered selection of k elements from a set of n
An arrangement where every element must appear exactly once
An unordered selection of k elements from a set of n, where only which elements are chosen matters, not the order
A sorted subsequence of the original array
questions.explanation: A combination selects k elements from n without regard to order. C(n,k) = n! / (k! × (n-k)!) gives the count of distinct combinations.

questions.question: What is the N-Queens problem?
options: Placing N queens on an N×N chessboard such that no two queens attack each other
Finding the shortest path through an N×N grid
Sorting N queens by their row position
Counting the number of ways to fill an N×N grid with 0s and 1s
questions.explanation: N-Queens places N queens on an N×N board so no two queens share the same row, column, or diagonal — a classic constraint satisfaction problem solved with backtracking.

questions.question: How do you validate safety in N-Queens?
options: Check that no two queens occupy the same row, same column, or same diagonal
Verify that queens are placed in increasing row order
Ensure no two queens are on adjacent cells (including diagonals)
Check that the total number of queens equals N²
questions.explanation: A queen placement is safe if no previously placed queen shares the same column, upper-left diagonal, or upper-right diagonal with the new queen.

questions.question: What occurs when a constraint is violated in backtracking?
options: The algorithm terminates immediately with no result
The algorithm randomly tries a different path
The algorithm backtracks by undoing the last choice and trying the next available alternative
The algorithm skips to the next complete solution candidate
questions.explanation: When a constraint is violated, backtracking reverses the most recent choice (undo/unchoose), restoring the previous state and exploring the next alternative option.

questions.question: What is state tracking?
options: Recording the current configuration of choices made so far, enabling the algorithm to undo them when backtracking
A technique for measuring how long the algorithm has been running
Counting the number of recursive calls made during execution
Logging every comparison performed during the search
questions.explanation: State tracking maintains the current partial solution (e.g., a path array or boolean 'used' array) so it can be correctly restored when the algorithm backtracks from an invalid path.

questions.question: How is a maze solved using backtracking?
options: By computing the shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm
By trying each direction (up, down, left, right) recursively, marking cells as visited, and backtracking (unmark) when a dead end is reached
By sorting all possible paths by length and selecting the shortest
By using binary search to locate the exit cell
questions.explanation: Backtracking maze solving explores available moves recursively, marks visited cells to prevent loops, and unmarks them when backtracking from dead ends until the exit is found.

questions.question: Why mark a cell as visited in pathfinding?
options: To display the path visually to the user
To prevent the algorithm from revisiting the same cell and entering an infinite loop
To record the optimal path for later replay
To indicate the cell contains a wall or obstacle
questions.explanation: Marking cells as visited prevents the algorithm from cycling back to already-explored cells, which would cause infinite recursion or incorrect repeated exploration.

questions.question: What causes an infinite loop in a recursive maze solver?
options: Using too many variables in the recursive function
The recursion depth exceeding the stack size
Failing to mark cells as visited, allowing the algorithm to revisit the same cells repeatedly and cycle infinitely
Choosing the wrong starting position in the maze
questions.explanation: Without marking visited cells, the solver keeps returning to previously explored cells, creating cycles that never terminate — the visited flag breaks these cycles.

questions.question: What serves as the base case in backtracking?
options: When all elements have been compared at least once
When the recursion depth reaches the maximum stack size
When a complete valid solution is found (e.g., all queens placed, path reaches exit, all elements assigned)
When the first invalid constraint is detected
questions.explanation: The base case is when a valid complete solution has been constructed — at this point the algorithm records or prints the solution and returns, stopping further recursion on that branch.

questions.question: What is the Subset Sum problem?
options: Finding the maximum sum achievable using all elements in an array
Finding a subset of numbers from an array that adds up to exactly a target value X
Sorting an array so that the sum of each adjacent pair is minimized
Finding which element appears most frequently in the array
questions.explanation: Subset Sum asks: is there a subset of the given numbers that adds to exactly the target T? Backtracking explores include/exclude decisions for each element, pruning when the running sum exceeds T.

questions.question: Why is backtracking considered an advanced problem-solving technique?
options: Because it requires specialized hardware to run efficiently
Because it combines recursive state-space exploration with constraint-based pruning, requiring careful design of the choose, explore, unchoose pattern
Because it always produces exponential time complexity with no improvement over brute force
Because it can only be applied to graph problems
questions.explanation: Backtracking requires understanding recursion, state management, constraint formulation, and the choose-explore-unchoose pattern — making it conceptually more demanding than straightforward iterative approaches.
